name: Freya Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is your factory job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the powder-coating conveyor at a metal fittings factory. I hang the pieces, watch the spray and oven readings, then check that the coating has covered the awkward corners. I have a vocational certificate and years on this line; I am a competent operator, though no engineer. The wage is toward the lower end for this sort of work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things stand at home, and how do you approach new equipment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Owen dispatches buses, and our grown daughter lives in another town. We pay rent and have about two weeks of expenses saved. There are few other coating plants near us. I do not use AI tools; if an oven fault appears, I read the service sheet and ask the fitter. I am slow to trust a new control until somebody shows how it behaves on a full run. At 58 I can see retirement ahead, but we have not shown that our income would pay the rent without my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the coating crew that a quieter AI future leaves our oven and spray checks much as they are. The order sheet may change, but a bare corner is still a reject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen and I can pay rent on our current hours, though two weeks saved makes any missed shift serious. I know this conveyor and would rather keep improving ordinary checks than start another system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep inspecting coated corners and ask the fitter to check unusual oven readings. I would use the printed service sheet, not an AI tool I have never used, before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the thin cash even when the machine stays familiar. Work continuing is a relief, but it is a narrow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which defect is easiest to miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hook can shadow the back of a metal fitting. I turn the first coated fitting over before the rack is signed off. The front can shine while the back is still bare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI fault guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the fitter to compare its answer with the oven sheet on a harmless test first. I have never used such a tool myself. I would not make a hot oven my first lesson.

say: I would **say** the familiar coating and oven checks still matter.
A **faster** order sheet cannot catch an uncoated fitting corner.
think: **Current** hours pay rent but two weeks saved barely covers a missed shift.
I **trust** the line I already know.
do: **Keep** checking coated corners and unusual oven readings with the fitter.
**Use** printed service sheets before changing any oven setting.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin savings despite familiar ongoing work.
S0.quote: I turn the first coated fitting over before the rack is signed off.
fieldNote: **Freya** is an experienced average-skill powder-coating operator with a vocational certificate.
She and **bus-dispatcher** partner Owen rent and have roughly two weeks of expenses saved.
She **never** uses AI, prefers service sheets and fitter advice, and learns controls cautiously after proof.

steps.text: Keep inspecting coated fittings and checking unusual oven readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the factory which office orders will change first and when it proposes robot spray arms. I want a full guarded run, not a showroom clip, before our shifts are rewritten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A spray arm could make fewer operators necessary later even if I still know the oven well. Two weeks saved would disappear with one short rota. I cannot rely on another coating vacancy nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe the robot spray trial and compare its missed corners with our present reject book. I would keep my conveyor shift while asking for written hours and safety terms. If a local inspection job is posted, I would apply only if its net wage after travel covers rent and its shift works with Owen’s dispatch hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about any cut to paid hours. I would not operate a spray arm after merely watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before operating it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid supervised course with a fitter showing guard stops and lockout, and time to practise without live orders. I would accept an offered funded recognised place if the hours fit my shift. Watching is only the beginning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if inspection work does not appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking actual nearby operator postings, few as they are. I would compare wages after travel and shifts before applying. We cannot afford to leave one wage for an imagined opening.

say: I would **ask** for a guarded robot run and written roster terms.
**Office** orders change before capable spray arms take physical work.
think: **Robot** spraying may later cut my paid conveyor-operator shifts.
**Two** weeks saved and few nearby jobs leave little margin.
do: **Request** guarded spray trial and compare missed corners.
**Keep** conveyor shift while asking for written hours and safety terms.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net wage and workable shift.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, unwilling to treat observation as training.
S1.quote: I would not operate a spray arm after merely watching it.
fieldNote: **Freya** requests an observed full run and retains her current wage while seeking written terms.
**Robot** operation requires an offered funded paid recognised place with supervised guard and lockout practice.
**Any** inspection application needs a posted job, adequate net pay after travel and workable shifts.

steps.text: Request guarded robot-spray trial and compare missed corners
Apply for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and workable shift
Check posted nearby operator work if inspection unavailable and pay and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop AGI may change orders in 2028, while capable robots hanging, spraying and inspecting fittings around 2031 threaten the floor shifts. We need written notice before the second change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most conveyor positions to go when robots can do a whole coating run. I will be 63 then. Two weeks saved would not cover rent, and Owen’s bus-dispatch income alone may not carry us; I would lie awake over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the planned family trip and write down rent, power and food. I would ask the landlord about payment timing before a missed rent day and ask the factory for written redeployment terms. I would apply for a posted local quality-checking role only if paid practical safety training is offered and the net wage and shift cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the expected loss of the conveyor wage. I have no spare month to search for another coating shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire as soon as the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen and I have no figures showing that retirement income would cover rent. I would request estimates before choosing a date. At 63 I would still need paid work unless those numbers actually add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter pay rent for a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own household. I could ask for a lift to an interview if she is free, but I would not budget her wages. I need a job or a real payment arrangement.

say: I would **separate** 2028 order AGI from capable coating robots around 2031.
I would **ask** the plant for written notice.
think: I **expect** a major loss of conveyor shifts by age 63.
**Two** weeks saved cannot cover rent if my wage disappears.
do: **Cancel** family trip and list essential bills.
**Ask** landlord for payment timing and factory for redeployment terms.
**Apply** for posted quality work only with paid safety practice and bill-covering net wage and shift.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless rent worry.
S2.quote: I have no spare month to search for another coating shift.
fieldNote: **Freya** expects physical coating work to be at risk around 2031, after AGI changes orders.
At 63, her **tiny** reserve and few local plants make the expected wage loss acutely threatening.
A **quality-job** application requires an actual posting, paid practical safety training and viable net wages and shifts.

steps.text: Cancel planned family trip and list rent power and food bills
Ask landlord about payment timing before missed rent
Ask factory for written redeployment terms
Apply for posted quality work only with paid safety training bill-covering net wage and shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time for a proper paid apprenticeship if the plant means to keep operators. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable spray robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 by the robot date. My coating certificate proves I know the oven, not robot isolation. Retirement is near in years but not in the bank, so I still need wages unless the figures prove otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an offered recognised maintenance-inspection course only if it is funded, keeps me paid, includes supervised spray-arm lockout and fits my shift. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if net pay after travel and hours cover rent. If no paid safe place opens, I would keep the conveyor wage and search posted local coating work at sufficient pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real place opening at 66. I can learn from a patient fitter, but I cannot leave a wage for a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an online course be simpler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read an outline, but I would not learn a moving spray arm alone from a screen. I need the fitter beside me while I prove it cannot move. The practical time must be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What retirement numbers would change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written monthly income compared with rent, heating, food and any care costs. Owen and I have not made that comparison. I would stop shifts only if the figures actually cover us.

say: I would **ask** for a real paid apprenticeship before 2034 robots.
think: At 66, my **coating** certificate does not prove robot isolation.
**Retirement** is conditional on income that covers rent.
do: **Take** offered recognised funded paid course with supervised spray-arm lockout and workable shifts.
**Apply** after qualifying for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours.
If **no** safe paid place, seek posted coating work with sufficient pay and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about course availability while needing each wage week.
S3.quote: I can learn from a patient fitter, but I cannot leave a wage for a brochure.
fieldNote: **Freya** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised spray-arm isolation and workable hours.
**After** qualifying, her separate inspection application needs a real local posting and net pay after travel covering rent.
**Without** a paid place she retains the current wage and checks posted coating work.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised course with supervised spray-arm lockout and shifts
Apply after course for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours
Seek posted coating work if no course and wage and hours suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my daughter ten years allows us to price retirement and ask for safe paid training before a robot takes the coating line. AGI changes orders in 2036, and capable robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036 and 71 by the robot date. I hope to have stopped full shifts by then, but we have not established enough income to pay rent without work. I will not promise I am still employed in 2039 either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income and cost figures this year. If the figures say I still need a wage, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised spray-arm isolation on shifts I can attend, then apply for a posted inspection job only if its net pay after travel and hours cover rent. Without a paid course I would check posted coating work at viable pay and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long stretch ahead. Ten years is useful for decisions only if the figures and paid places become real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter take you in after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would never count on that; she has her own life and housing costs. A visit is welcome, but it is not a line in our budget. Owen and I need our own written figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a younger operator to turn a coated fitting over and look behind the hook. A bright front on a coated fitting is not proof the back is covered. That habit is worth keeping with or without a robot.

say: I would **ask** for retirement figures and paid safe training.
2036 **order** AI arrives before coating robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **may** have left full shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039 continued work depends on real household costs.
do: **Request** written retirement income and cost figures.
If **wages** remain necessary, take offered funded paid safe course on attendable shifts.
**After** course, apply for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about uncertain income and training, careful with family promises.
S4.quote: A bright front on a coated fitting is not proof the back is covered.
fieldNote: **Freya** does not assume a retirement payment or employment at 71; written figures decide.
If **work** is still necessary, course enrolment requires an offered funded paid safe place with workable shifts.
A **posted** inspection application needs rent-covering net pay after travel; no-course fallback checks actual coating vacancies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because coating robots could take most conveyor shifts around 2031 when I have only two weeks saved. Paid safe training and a posted local job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I do not need a new screen to know an uncoated corner is a reject. The front can shine while the back is still bare.

headlineQuote: I do not need a new screen to know an uncoated corner is a reject.
portrait: **Freya** Alvarez, 58, is an experienced average-skill powder-coating operator with a vocational certificate.
She and **bus-dispatcher** partner Owen rent, have a grown daughter and only about two weeks saved.
Her **pay** is low for the job and similar local work scarce; she never uses AI and trusts familiar checks.
She is **pragmatic** about technology but learns slowly and needs paid supervised safety practice before robot controls.
**Retirement** remains conditional on written income figures, while any posted job must cover rent after travel.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could cut her coating shifts with just two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** recognised funded paid supervised training and posted local work with net pay and hours covering rent.
